talks.title: Let Them Eat Cake
talks.teaser: Examines why small and medium businesses struggle with security tooling and argues vendors should build secure-by-default products.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens by acknowledging the land and then defines small and medium businesses as firms with under a thousand employees and under a billion dollars in annual revenue. The speaker argues that these businesses drive a large share of the economy and spend heavily on technology, yet the security industry is built around large enterprises. Most of them have no IT or security staff, so advice about DevSecOps and shift-left practices is out of reach for them.

The middle of the talk looks at how these businesses buy and run security. Purchasing tends to follow word of mouth and free trials rather than formal evaluation, and buyers want centralized marketplaces for comparison. The speaker describes a "security tax" in which single sign-on and advanced features cost substantially more, using GitHub and common collaboration tools as examples. Typical gaps include missing multi-factor authentication, excessive administrator rights and no logging. Ransomware is presented as a threat that hits small organizations as hard as large ones, since attackers do not screen by size, and AI tools are described as too unreliable to replace human risk assessment.

The closing section turns to software liability regulation. The speaker admits she once opposed it, explains how shared responsibility models can shift blame onto customers, and compares the situation to seat belts, which became mandatory only after decades of availability. The takeaway is that vendors should ship products that are secure by default. Attendees at larger companies were encouraged to press their leadership to make security features more affordable for smaller customers.

talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Explores how AI could close the coverage, context and communication gaps behind security leaders' recurring problems.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with an analogy between human learning and large language models. People move information from short-term memory to working memory, then to specialized and foundational knowledge. LLMs have separate stages instead: the context window, retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning and the base model. The speaker argues that automating the movement between these stages is a central goal, and that smaller local models and faster chips will make real-time, increasingly autonomous AI practical.

Turning to enterprises, the speaker predicts that meetings will be recorded and searchable, documentation will update itself, status reporting will be automated, and models embedded in production systems will detect and fix problems. The persistent challenges facing security leaders are reporting, vulnerability management, least privilege, measurement, third-party incidents and detection and response. The speaker attributes them to three root issues: coverage, context and communication. A story about an unexpected public S3 bucket shows how hard it is to establish ownership and intent without broad visibility.

The talk closes with examples of how AI could attach context to alerts, support triage and translate findings for different audiences. On data risk, the speaker argues that leakage from a model itself is often overstated, but warns that sensitive material placed in vector databases can be returned to users. Enterprises should clean data before ingesting it, and training data poisoning is a real concern that has no settled fix.

talks.title: Patch Perfect: Harmonizing with LLMs to Find Security Vulns
talks.teaser: Shows how an LLM can rank changed functions in a patch diff to locate the code that fixes a disclosed vulnerability.
talks.summary:
The talk examines whether large language models help with N-day vulnerability research, focusing on patch diffing. The speakers frame the question as whether LLMs are a real leap forward or mostly sophisticated autocomplete, and they limit the scope to static analysis of decompiled code taken from binary diffs. They begin with an overview of recent academic work, noting that a general-purpose model tended to outperform specialised ones and that giving the model the vulnerability description strongly affected results.

The core of the talk walks through an iterative workflow built against a Citrix advisory, then a Checkpoint gateway bug. Early prompts produced inflated scores, even for changes that only renamed variables. The team improved results by filtering out unrelated components, summarising security-relevant logic before scoring, combining two diffing tools, and running a final ranking pass. Because output varied between runs, they sampled small groups of functions repeatedly and averaged the placements, which they called multi-sample sorting. In the Checkpoint case the fixed function landed in the top ten percent of roughly 300 changed functions.

The closing section covers limitations and takeaways. Context window size and non-determinism remained the main constraints, and a few outlier runs still skewed individual results. The speakers argue that LLMs can give an analyst a better starting point for manual triage rather than replace analysis. They suggest future work such as adding call-tree context, using agents for dynamic testing, and retrieving product documentation to inform the ranking.

talks.title: Its Coming From Inside the House: Guide to Physical Facility Pentesting
talks.teaser: Walks through planning and carrying out physical penetration tests, from reconnaissance and pretexting to badge cloning.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with scoping a physical facility engagement. The speaker stresses agreeing on in-scope methods, success criteria and after-hours contacts, and using a letter of authorization plus a third-party consent form when the client does not own the building. Reconnaissance comes next: social media, company hashtags and satellite imagery can reveal badge designs, dress codes and entry points, and on-site visits confirm what remote research suggested, including crowd flow and the security culture of staff.

The middle section covers initial access through three routes: social engineering with tailgating, surreptitious entry outside business hours, and authenticated entry by badge cloning. The speaker explains how to build a pretext that gets you in, lets you move around and lets you stay, and how inexpensive replica badges can be made. Badge technology is traced from magnetic stripe through low-frequency and high-frequency RFID to newer readers, with notes on which formats are vulnerable and on tools such as Flipper Zero and Proxmark. A covert reader placed beside a door can capture credentials from people who badge in.

The talk closes with post-exploitation: photograph evidence, stay within the agreed impact, and leave the site no less secure than it was found. The main takeaway is that preparation, documentation and a calm, credible story matter most.

talks.title: The ABCs of DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Introduces core DevSecOps concepts across the application lifecycle and where security controls belong at each stage.
talks.summary:
Application security is often neglected while development teams prioritize shipping new features, and fixes tend to arrive only after a breach or an audit finding. The session treats this as a problem to solve across the whole application lifecycle rather than at the end. It starts with a plain explanation of DevOps as an iterative, merged cycle of planning, coding, building, testing, releasing, operating and monitoring, and argues that collaboration and automation make that cycle work.

The middle of the talk maps security controls onto each stage. Threat modeling during planning, using frameworks such as STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK, comes first. Then come IDE plugins and pre-commit hooks, static analysis during the build, and software composition analysis to catch known flaws in third-party libraries. Once software is deployed, dynamic testing, container and infrastructure scanning, runtime monitoring, feature flags and rollback come into play. The speaker stresses that a defect found during requirements costs far less to fix than one found in production, and uses that point to make the business case.

The closing section covers governance. The CISO should define the implementation model and target maturity, while the business decides how much to spend on tooling. OWASP's DevSecOps verification standard and maturity model, DoD guidance and NIST's software supply chain work are offered as references. The main takeaway is to start small, for example by running a free static analysis scanner, and to secure executive backing and developer buy-in alongside the tools.

talks.title: My Way is Not Very Sportsman-Like
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders can shape attacker behavior using the Pyramid of Pain and deception rather than accepting the Defender's Dilemma.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by challenging the "Defender's Dilemma," the common belief that defenders must get everything right while attackers need only one success. The speaker argues this premise is outdated and leads teams to poor spending decisions and demoralized staff. Intrusions unfold across a lifecycle with many points where activity can be detected and interrupted, not a single event, so defenders have chances to act at several stages.

The middle of the talk turns to the defender's first-move advantage. Defenders can prepare the environment before an adversary acts, and basic hygiene such as multifactor authentication, patching, asset inventory and software bill of materials is framed as setting the board. The speaker then walks through the Pyramid of Pain, showing that detecting hashes, IP addresses and domains is cheap for adversaries to dodge, while detecting tools and behaviors imposes real cost. Resilience, proactive threat hunting and deception, such as canary tokens, decoy accounts and honeypots, are presented as further ways to waste attacker time and slow their progress.

The closing argument is for an "attacker's dilemma" mindset, in which adversaries must avoid errors across their entire lifecycle. The speaker encourages practitioners to look for opportunities in their own daily work to shape attacker choices, and to build defenses that are inexpensive yet force mistakes.

talks.title: That Shouldn't Have Worked - Payload Development 101
talks.teaser: Covers methods red teamers use on engagements to get payloads past modern defenses and detections.

talks.title: Consumer Routers Still Suck
talks.teaser: Surveys years of consumer router and ISP device flaws, showing repeated bug classes and tangled vendor supply chains behind them.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through several years of offensive research on consumer routers and networking gear, from mainstream Netgear and TP-Link models to ISP-supplied modems and newer app-managed devices. The presenters describe their approach to each device: find debug ports, get a shell, pull the firmware, then hunt for bugs. Many of the flaws were old bug classes such as command injection, buffer overflows, format strings, and missing CSRF checks, and some devices exposed services over IPv6 that the vendors had not accounted for.

A recurring theme is the supply chain. Shared firmware from one original manufacturer, such as code reused across ISPs and brands, meant a single flaw could affect many vendors across several countries. A path traversal in Buffalo routers traced back to code that dated to the mid-2000s. Other examples included a VPN feature in an app-managed router that exposed other customers' networks, a cloud management API with an object reference flaw that returned after being fixed, and a vendor SDK bug inherited from a chipset maker. The talk also covers botnets and threat groups using compromised home routers as proxies, and a mass bricking event.

The closing argument is that these devices keep failing because of unclear ownership and tangled supply chains, which make disclosure hard. The presenters point to software bills of materials and regulation as partial fixes, and suggest that consumer routers are a low-cost place to learn offensive techniques using common reverse engineering and web testing tools.

talks.title: Prioritization Myths Busted with Better Vulnerability Data
talks.teaser: Compares EPSS and CVSS scoring and proposes a transparent method for ranking which vulnerabilities to fix first.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a data scientist at a vulnerability intelligence company, opens with a lunch-picking analogy to frame prioritization as sorting and filtering options against a goal or constraint. For vulnerabilities, he argues the core aim is avoiding exploitation. He notes that the gap between disclosure and public exploit keeps shrinking, and that the NVD has stopped supplying the metadata teams need to rank flaws.

He then compares scoring approaches. EPSS estimates exploitation likelihood and performs well, but its latest model is effectively a black box that cannot be audited or easily explained. CVSS is transparent and flexible, yet its highest bands hold roughly as many vulnerabilities as teams can realistically fix, so it does not order the top group. He warns that signals such as KEV listing, social attention and EPSS can reinforce one another, inflating a single flaw's prominence. His proposal is to rank available metadata by importance, then keep the vulnerabilities that are not outclassed on the most important factors, using Pareto-style tiers that combine transparent and complex scores.

In the question period the discussion moved to the number of affected systems, unreliable CPE naming, and reputational or political pressure that can override scores. The takeaways are to combine several signals, be skeptical of unanimous agreement, and invest in knowing your assets.

talks.title: Hacking Exchange From The Outside In
talks.teaser: Explains how fuzzing Oracle Outside In file parsers used by Exchange surfaced memory corruption bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Microsoft Exchange Server 2019, which uses Oracle's Outside In libraries to parse file types attached to emails. The presenter explains why this C++ SDK, which supports over 600 formats, suited memory corruption research. Fuzzer families are compared, from dumb and grammar-based tools to mutation and coverage-guided ones, before explaining the choice of AFL on Linux and Jackalope with TinyInst on Windows.

Windows fuzzing relied on GFlags page heap, which adds guard pages around allocations so overflows and use-after-free accesses fault immediately. Harness changes such as shared memory and persistent mode raised execution speed. Across three libraries, the PDF and Excel parsers yielded far more crashes than HTML, including stack overflows, heap out-of-bounds reads and flawed bounds checks. One HTML use-after-free was minimised and traced to a tree node destructor that mishandled the rightmost child.

Lab setup needed a domain controller, static addresses and mail flow rules that route attachments to the scanning process, plus raised memory limits in its configuration. Attaching a debugger to the process that loads the HTML library made crash triage possible. Reporting took months: Microsoft initially omitted credit and bounty, Oracle released a patch, and Microsoft later announced it would retire the product. The main takeaway is that legacy parsing code is under-tested and that fuzzing it is more accessible than it looks.

talks.title: Some Assembly Required: Weaponizing Chrome CVE-2023-2033 for RCE in Electron
talks.teaser: Shows how a public V8 type confusion bug was turned into working remote code execution in an Electron renderer.
talks.summary:
The talk follows the development of a remote code execution exploit for CVE-2023-2033, a type confusion bug in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine. The work began during a bug bounty engagement against an Electron desktop client running an outdated Chrome build, where a working proof of concept was needed to demonstrate real impact. No public full RCE exploit existed for this bug, so the research started from existing proof-of-concept code that provided V8 heap read, write and address-of primitives.

The speaker first had to make those primitives install reliably on a production Chrome build rather than a developer shell, which required adjusting the script and retrying it. The exploit then redirected a function's JIT code pointer into shellcode hidden inside float64 constants that the optimizing compiler emitted as immediate-load instructions. Getting longer payloads to run meant working around compiler optimizations that merged repeated shellcode chunks, and accounting for x86-64 instruction size changes that shifted the jump offsets. The final payload fetched and ran a remote shell script inside an unsandboxed renderer, and several parallel instances of the exploit were used to improve reliability.

The main takeaway is that a public browser proof of concept can be turned into a working exploit with substantial debugging, and that a renderer running without the Chrome sandbox gives an attacker far more room. The speaker reported the issue through a bug bounty program and received a critical payout, though the vendor's response focused on the cross-site scripting bug used to reach the vulnerable component.

talks.title: Embracing My Inner Cyber Wizard To Defeat Impostor Syndrome
talks.teaser: Shows how a personal hacker grimoire and documentation habits can help security professionals counter impostor syndrome.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining impostor syndrome as persistent self-doubt among high-achieving people, even when objective evidence shows their success. It traces the concept back to 1970s research and notes that it has no clear-cut clinical diagnosis. The speaker then describes why information security staff are especially exposed to it: a constant stream of new threats, a crowded vendor landscape, and broad technical domains they are expected to master, often with small teams.

The middle of the talk introduces the "hacker grimoire," a personal reference notebook or digital repository of technical notes, commands and procedures. The speaker uses fantasy and science fiction imagery, hacker-culture films and the 2600 magazine to motivate the idea, and shows photos of their own notebook. Practical guidance covers keeping it easy to reach, defining acronyms so they remain understandable later, never storing real passwords, and using shorthand you can maintain. Recording accomplishments in it also helps with performance reviews.

The closing advice focuses on coping strategies: finding a niche, avoiding constant comparison with colleagues, talking with peers and professional groups, taking time off, and treating therapy as a normal option. For organizations, the speaker suggests encouraging personal documentation so institutional knowledge is not lost when people leave. The main takeaway is that writing down what you learn and accomplish builds confidence, and that struggling with impostor feelings is common across the field.

talks.title: Unlocking Generative AI: Balancing Innovation with Security
talks.teaser: Surveys generative AI risks for enterprises, from prompt injection and data poisoning to model theft, with mitigation ideas.
talks.summary:
Jason Ross opens by framing generative AI as a technology that produces new content rather than retrieving or predicting it. He highlights two traits that matter for organizations: outputs are non-deterministic, so the same input can yield different results, and the content is persuasive enough that people tend to accept it without checking. He walks through common corporate uses such as marketing, internal search, meeting summaries, build reporting and incident reporting, and explains how hallucinations and data exposure can creep into each.

The middle of the talk follows the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications. Ross covers prompt injection, arguing that the real concern is data exposure rather than offensive text, along with model theft, data poisoning and excessive agency. He notes that poisoning increasingly happens through retrieval-augmented generation data stores and internal wikis rather than the model itself, and that model files can behave like code, so supply chain risk spans the whole stack. He also raises the difficulty of honoring deletion requests once data has been trained into a model.

For defenders, the takeaway is that general application security still applies, but training environments should be treated as production, training data needs vetting, and model artifacts should be compared against known good versions. Legal contracts with model providers and ethics review become part of the security program. Ross closes by noting that model output can change between versions and that the OWASP list is being revised with community input.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering for Dummies: The “what if?” User
talks.teaser: Shows how a curious user reverse engineers an Android game, a product waitlist, and a pub/sub system to find design flaws.
talks.summary:
Micah Parks explores the "what if?" user, someone who uses a product in ways its builders did not intend, such as spotting an embedded key or an unprotected endpoint. He revisits three older, low-stakes projects where he took that role, then advises the tech lead on fixes.

The first case is an Android word game built with Unity. Extracting its word list from the game's data file let him build a solver that beat his partner, and he suggested obfuscation or license checks as optional hardening. The second is a waitlist for exercise equipment. A resale listing exposed a direct product link, and scraping predictable, sequential URLs revealed other waitlisted items. He recommended random identifiers, rate limits and a web application firewall.

The third case involves an auction site whose real-time messaging feed sent every visitor the top bids of all bidders, along with some personal data, because subscriber keys and channels were too broadly scoped. That information would let a seller capture maximum bids. Takeaways include limiting channels to what each user needs, keeping sensitive fields off the client, and reviewing console output before deployment.

talks.title: Apples to Apples
talks.teaser: Shows buyers how to compare security service bids and deliverables so a penetration test delivers real value.
talks.summary:
Luke McOmie, a long-time penetration tester who later ran security practices as an executive, argues that organizations often spend large budgets on security services that do little to improve their posture. He points to a gap between the people doing the work, the people buying it, and the firms selling it, and says scoping, bidding and reporting are where buyers usually lose value.

He walks through three real engagements. An insurance company that started with a routine annual test moved to a programmatic approach with continuous assessment, and its accepted risk dropped sharply. A large outdoor entertainment company ran a long RFP, chose the cheapest qualified bidder, and got a repeat of work it had already done, followed by a phishing compromise. A software firm that had been compromised paid for a thorough test that reached domain administrator access within minutes, which its previous cheaper provider had missed. He also covers how PCI scopes are often tested only from outside, how templated scanner output and padded reports fail to show impact, and how insurers may reject such work.

He closes with practical advice: ask for a sample deliverable before buying, require hours and hourly rates broken out in the bid, confirm which consultants will do the work, hold a recap call after each meeting, and expect testers to go beyond the first default attack path. Buyers should drive the scope from their own risk goals rather than from checkbox requirements.

talks.title: Defending Against the Deep: Is your workforce ready Gen AI Adversaries?
talks.teaser: Explores how generative AI media fuels deepfake fraud and voice phishing, and how staff can learn to spot it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining AI-generated media and tracing how generative tools moved from research into everyday software. The speaker argues that AI is now built into most products and that attackers can use it just as easily as defenders. Recent incidents frame the risk: a deepfaked video call with fake executives that led to a large fraudulent payment, and cloned voices used to talk a help desk into resetting credentials, which opened the door to a ransomware attack.

The core of the session is a live quiz in which attendees voted on which sample was AI-generated, covering text, support tickets, images, audio and video. The speaker showed that text and images are getting harder to judge, that AI detectors make mistakes, and that searching for an original source is a practical check. Cues for audio and video include breathing artifacts, odd pronunciation, unnatural repeated gestures and delayed responses. Demonstrations then showed how quickly a short promotional video, a voice clone built from a few minutes of footage, and multi-language dubbing could be produced, along with limits such as poor input quality and longer clips drifting into repetition.

To close, the speaker recommended building workforce awareness through regular, gamified quizzes, hands-on exercises and continuous learning, along with verifying unusual requests through an independent channel. The takeaway is that verification habits and critical thinking matter more than the ability to spot a perfect fake.

talks.title: Social Engineering the Social Engineers: How To Not Suck at Buying Software
talks.teaser: Explains how security tools are bought and sold, and where buyers and sellers commonly go wrong.
talks.summary:
David Girvin opens with his move from hands-on offensive security into the vendor side, going from pen testing and security leadership roles to working as a sales engineer. He frames the talk as a look at how security tools get purchased, seen from both the buyer's seat and the seller's, and argues that each side misreads the other's incentives. He walks through the sales pipeline in order: prospecting by sales development reps, discovery calls, proof-of-value trials, executive alignment, and procurement and pricing. Along the way he explains how compensation shapes behavior and why pricing complex platforms takes real discovery work.

The middle of the talk focuses on pitfalls. Buyers are urged to build a scorecard before evaluating, to confirm they have data access and staff time for a proof of value, and to define scope and success criteria in a shared document. He warns against vague marketing claims, hidden costs, curated sandbox trials that do not reflect real conditions, and buying one broad tool on the promise that it fixes everything. He also recommends asking partners and resellers whose interests they actually serve.

He closes by urging buyers to be candid about budget and decision authority, and sellers to be open about product limits. The takeaway is that a mutually beneficial deal holds up better than one won through pressure, and that a practitioner who understands the other side's constraints can negotiate outcomes that work for everyone involved.

talks.title: Please Waste My Time
talks.teaser: Shows defenders how honeypots, decoy accounts and tripwires can slow attackers and reveal their activity inside Windows networks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a red teamer's view of why Windows enterprise networks are hard to secure. The speaker walks through the weaknesses pentesters rely on: broadcast name resolution poisoning that captures NTLM challenge responses, relaying those authentications to hosts without SMB signing, Kerberoasting service accounts with weak passwords, and reusing local administrator hashes across machines. Each one traces back to a default setting or a common bad practice.

The middle of the talk turns to deception. Ideas include a honey user that looks like a real account and should never be touched, a decoy service principal name that alerts when a ticket is requested, alerts on RC4 ticket requests in an AES-only environment, and fake or disabled local admin accounts planted where credential dumping will find them. Canary tokens embedded in documents on file shares can report when someone opens them. The speaker also shares a small PowerShell tool, built with an AI assistant, that sends decoy name-resolution requests and flags any host that answers, which points to responder-style tooling on the network. Fake documentation and password databases can misdirect intruders as well.

The closing part covers rollout. The speaker recommends starting with a single honeypot, tuning alerts so they only fire on real activity, and not treating deployment as a reason to skip other security work. Legacy systems and backward-compatibility needs slow the move to newer defaults, so many of these weaknesses remain in place.

talks.title: Secure Legends GameDay - A Cloud Security Danger Room
talks.teaser: Walks attendees through a live AWS incident response exercise, from isolating compromised instances to blocking an attack path.
talks.summary:
This session is a hands-on AWS "game day," a simulated incident set at a fictional startup, Unicorn.Rentals. Attendees with laptops could join a live environment in their own AWS account. The scenario is a set of EC2 instances behind a load balancer whose content has been encrypted, with a ransom message left on the site. The speaker presents the exercise as a low-pressure way to build response experience that is hard to get during a real outage.

The group works through detection and analysis first, then containment, eradication and recovery. Load balancer metrics and networking options are considered, but the instance logs prove most useful. They reveal requests to a "backdoor" route that appears to run arbitrary shell commands on the server. The team isolates an affected instance by swapping its security group for one with no inbound rules, then blocks the route at the application load balancer with a fixed response. The vulnerable code stays in place for later review. The autoscaling group, driven by its launch template, replaces the encrypted instances, which are stopped rather than terminated so evidence is preserved.

The main takeaways are to follow the runbook in order, since the team skipped isolation at first, and to contain before eradicating. Deleting resources during an active attack destroys evidence that forensics will need. Blocking an endpoint at the edge buys time but does not remove the underlying backdoor. Involving the team that owns a resource before changing it is also part of the lesson.

talks.title: Verified for Business Continuity: How to Remediate Risk Across Enterprise
talks.teaser: Shows how existing security tools can close exposures and block attackers without disrupting business operations.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a security practitioner and company founder with a long background in offense and defense, opens with the tension at the heart of remediation: security changes can break business systems, and a policy pushed late in the week can cause weekend outages. Many organizations can scan for exposures, and some already own the tools to do so, but knowing about a flaw is different from fixing it. Patching every system quickly is rarely realistic, so the talk looks at other ways to reduce risk.

The middle of the talk walks through practical examples. One is a registry-level Windows configuration change that removes the exposure from a recently disclosed Office-related exploit path without requiring a restart. Another covers using firewall and security logs to find the sources of blocked attacks, then pushing those indicators to other controls in the environment, with the caution that blocking individual IP addresses does not scale. The speaker also highlights common misconfigurations in prevention products, such as features left in detect-only or staging mode and broad exclusions granted to internal teams, which quietly leave gaps even when the product appears fully deployed.

The closing takeaways focus on process. Teams should map which controls protect which hosts, prioritize the small set of vulnerabilities that compensating controls cannot cover, and validate changes through penetration testing or breach simulation. Before replacing a tool, they should weigh the disruption and cost against what they already own, and measure whether their controls are actually blocking what matters.

talks.title: API-ocalypse
talks.teaser: Walks through hands-on pentesting of a deliberately vulnerable API, showing authorization, mass assignment and injection flaws.
talks.summary:
Jennifer Shannon opens with a short primer on APIs, describing them as a way for web services to expose functions to other computers. She points to the OWASP API Top 10, noting that most of its entries involve authentication or authorization, and says API testing has grown from an occasional task into a routine part of her work.

The core of the talk is a live walkthrough against a deliberately vulnerable API running in a pentesting virtual machine. Using Postman to send requests and Burp Suite Community Edition to intercept and replay them, she works through a series of endpoints. Changing a user ID returns other people's accounts, which shows missing object-level authorization. Supplying extra fields when creating an account sets credits and an administrator flag, a mass assignment flaw. A crafted value in a login field bypasses the check and returns an admin token through SQL injection. An older versioned endpoint with a weak rate limit is shown to be brute-forceable.

She closes with audience questions. She says homegrown APIs fail far more often than carefully built ones, and compares REST with GraphQL, where batching and deeply nested queries bring denial-of-service and username enumeration risks. Her takeaways are to check authorization on every object, never trust client input, retire old API versions, and keep secrets such as API keys out of URLs.

talks.title: The Human Experience of Security Operations
talks.teaser: Argues security operations succeed or fail on people and process, drawing on two years of SOC leader and analyst interviews.
talks.summary:
Chris Tillett opens by mocking unrealistic security wish lists and vendor pitches that ignore the people who must carry them out. He describes customers who wanted password audits despite having no password policy, and conditional MFA rules that system administrators would quickly work around. His point is that the workforce's skills and habits should shape any tooling decision before a purchase is made.

The middle of the talk covers his team's experience running a security operations center with nine analysts handling a very large daily event volume. He explains how a tool-by-tool, alert-driven workflow proved slow, and how the team rebuilt its process around first-principles questions, better detections and clearer automation. He also walks through insider threat patterns, where a small group causes most of the trouble and layoffs can trigger data theft, and compares the work to warehouse and ERP operations to argue for process-focused redesign.

He closes by separating analytics, machine learning and generative AI, and by urging teams to tie security improvements to business outcomes they can measure. The practical takeaway is that staffing, analyst onboarding time and workflow design matter as much as the product stack, and that new capabilities should be judged against concrete operational needs.

talks.title: Mindfulness, Meditation, and Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Introduces mindfulness as a way to handle stress and burnout in security work, with a short guided practice.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing mindfulness as cultivating awareness, and compares it to situational awareness in security work. Drawing on years of teaching yoga and meditation before moving into penetration testing, the speaker argues that burnout is a widespread problem in cybersecurity and that these practices apply to people regardless of whether they are technical or non-technical.

The middle of the talk covers stress management and communication. Emotional self-awareness is presented as a learnable skill, and the speaker suggests asking whether a thought is true, whether it is real, and what other way there is to see the situation. Biases are discussed as things that become manageable once they are noticed. Listening and speaking from one's own needs are described as ways to reduce conflict, since many disagreements come from an unmet need. Compassion is framed as recognizing that everyone is part of a process with limited awareness.

The talk closes with a guided meditation of a few minutes. Attendees could choose an anchor such as the body, the breath, or thoughts, and they were invited to notice sensations and let them pass. Afterward the speaker observed that calm was present throughout, even when it was not felt. The main takeaway is that practice can be small and adapted to the moment, and that returning to it repeatedly matters more than doing it perfectly or on a fixed schedule.

talks.title: Orion's Quest: Navigating Cyber Wilderness - Tales of Modern Pentesting
talks.teaser: Shares real pentest stories on flawed web apps, captive portals, physical intrusion and phishing, and how to communicate risk.
talks.summary:
Kevin Johnson, founder of a penetration testing firm, argues that testers should explain how attacks happened rather than only list findings. He opens by criticizing the habit of treating techniques as secret and reports that give raw issue counts without a narrative of what was tested and why it matters to the business.

The middle of the talk walks through several engagements. A membership organization's registration flow exposed personal records through a predictable numeric identifier that could be changed to pull other members' data, and nothing monitored that unauthenticated path. A military contractor's guest wireless captive portal led to command execution, then to the internal domain after a network consolidation had merged guest and private infrastructure. Physical tests covered walking through a hospital and a bank data center, and a phishing exercise showed that a copied internal contact often clicked first. A scanner account with broad rights was also shown to expose more than expected.

The closing section turns to defenders. Johnson argues that security teams should first examine their own behavior, such as unlocked workstations, unnecessary admin rights and their own susceptibility to social engineering, and that users often spot breaches before tools do. The practical takeaway is to test your own registration and login flows, review applications that were built internally and may have been overlooked, and write reports that explain real risk.

talks.title: Scaling Your Creative Output with AI: Lessons from SANS Holiday Hack
talks.teaser: Surveys generative AI tools and shows how a CTF design team used them for game dialogue, art and voice.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a plain explanation of generative AI as a way of compressing language, images and audio into a compact representation and producing new output from it. It then surveys the tool landscape, from hosted commercial services to free open-source models and desktop applications that let people run models privately on their own hardware. Open models often ship without the safety guardrails found in commercial services, which the speaker flags as a topic worth discussing.

The middle section argues that a real project with a clear purpose is the best starting point, and that unexpected output can seed better ideas. Examples include a small web interface for comparing prompt variants and workflows for matching map tiles to photos. The main case study comes from the SANS Holiday Hack Challenge, where the design team used a language model to draft NPC dialogue from years of earlier lines, image models to produce map tiles and a set of whimsical fish artwork, and a text-to-speech pipeline to voice dialogue stored in a spreadsheet-driven game engine. The speaker estimated the dialogue tool roughly halved writing time, and more artists were able to contribute to the game's look.

The closing looks at the risks: lawsuits over training data are reshaping commercial tools, low-effort content will flood platforms, and cloned voices and images erode trust in media. The main takeaway is that communicating ideas is getting easier, so practitioners who pair AI with solid data and real projects should gain an edge.

talks.title: Improv Comedy for Social Engineering
talks.teaser: Teaches improv comedy exercises that build quick thinking, clear communication and composure for social engineering work.
talks.summary:
Ross Merritt, a security consultant with a background in improv comedy, opens by framing social engineering as a game. He argues that the mindset needed for pretext calls and phishing work resembles the one performers use on stage, and that the session would use improv training to build the fast reactions, presence and calm that help when operating in unfamiliar situations.

The workshop runs through a series of short group exercises. Zip Zap Zop trains attentive communication while tracking what is happening around you, and a ball-passing game adds a second object to test whether people can follow several things at once. The "yes, and" principle is presented as a way to absorb whatever a target says and build on it, rather than running into a dead end with yes-or-no questions. Volunteers also performed a three-sentence scene, where a short exchange had to reveal the relationship between two characters, practising rapport and adapting on the fly.

The closing message is that confidence and a willingness to look foolish matter more than a rehearsed script, and that failure is a normal part of improving. Attendees were encouraged to seek out a local improv group to keep building these skills, and the session ended with an open invitation for questions.

talks.title: Quickstart To Building Your Own Private AI Chat
talks.teaser: Shows how to run open-source language models locally and connect them to personal notes for a private AI chat setup.
talks.summary:
Sam Panicker opens by framing AI as something even experts do not fully understand, then argues for running models privately rather than relying only on public chat services. He describes the risks he sees with public models, including how easily adversarial prompting can push them off course, and explains why he runs models on his own hardware for work such as assessment notes and reporting.

The middle of the session is a live demo of free, open-source tooling. He walks through LM Studio and Ollama for downloading and serving open models from a model hub, then shows Open WebUI running in Docker as a chat front end. He connects the setup to an Obsidian notes vault so answers draw on his own documents, explains how text and images are split into chunks and turned into vector embeddings for retrieval, and touches on prompt patterns and using a model to generate API code.

He closes with a discussion of control: how a private model can be tuned without the guardrails a public service must enforce, and why that tradeoff matters. The takeaway is that local retrieval-augmented setups are now accessible to newcomers, but model behavior is still hard to predict, so decisions about access and guardrails deserve deliberate thought. The session ends with an open invitation for audience questions.

talks.title: Strategic Alliances: How GRC Teams Empower Offensive Security Efforts
talks.teaser: Shows how governance, risk and compliance teams can support offensive security through prioritization, policy alignment and shared communication.
talks.summary:
Darryl MacLeod, a GRC adviser, argues that governance, risk and compliance teams can strengthen offensive security work well beyond their usual role of writing policy, assessing controls and tracking risk. He opens by contrasting the two disciplines: penetration testing and red teaming on one side, and regulatory alignment, risk management and policy development on the other. He frames GRC as a partner that helps organizations rather than a checklist-driven obstacle.

The middle of the talk walks through ways the two teams can cooperate. GRC can tie testing to frameworks such as PCI DSS and NIST 800-53, shape test scope around regulated data and high-value systems, and review penetration test reports for compliance gaps. Risk assessments can set priorities, and red team results can feed back into risk registers and policy updates. He also covers focusing testing effort on the highest-risk systems, shared metrics, cross-training through internal exercises, threat modeling with GRC data, and keeping a central repository of documentation that both groups can use.

He closes with practical steps: set joint goals, hold regular meetings, share tools and processes, and involve offensive security in tabletop exercises and incident response planning. The takeaway for practitioners is that continuous feedback between the two teams produces a more unified security posture and makes results easier to explain to executives.

talks.title: Once Upon a Cyber Threat: The Brothers Grimms Teachings on APT Awareness
talks.teaser: Uses Brothers Grimm fairy tales to reframe advanced persistent threats as patient, people-driven attacks and social engineering.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by questioning the common picture of advanced persistent threats as nation-state actors working through exotic zero-days. The speaker argues that this label is too narrow, since a single person, a group of teenagers or an organized criminal crew can be just as persistent. Advanced is redefined as sustained effort, planning and patience rather than technical sophistication.

Using stories such as Snow White and a tale about a weaver's revenge, the talk walks through case studies in which an attacker builds trust, wears down a target and then strikes. The examples include a disgruntled developer who slowly takes know-how to a competitor, an impersonated support call that leads a user to install a remote-access tool, and a long, personalized spear-phishing campaign run by a state-linked group. The speaker also shows how automated tools can build tailored profiles of many people at once, and how public social media and property records can expose a family's routines and details.

The closing advice is to move away from annual videos and checklists. Instead, teams should run hands-on, individual exercises that show staff how much of their own information is exposed, and test defenses with realistic phishing and targeted messages. The talk argues that patient, realistic training costs far less than recovering from a breach.
